**Research note: PostgreSQL limits for schema and pool sizing**

**Identifier length.** By default PostgreSQL identifiers (table, column, index names and so on) can be at most 63 bytes. The lexical-structure documentation says "By default, NAMEDATALEN is 64 so the maximum identifier length is 63 bytes" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html). Longer names are accepted in commands but silently truncated. Two long generated names that share a prefix can therefore collide, which matters for auto-generated constraint and index names. The limit is in bytes, not characters, so multibyte UTF-8 names hit it sooner. The "Appendix: PostgreSQL Limits" page lists the same 63 bytes and notes it can be raised by recompiling (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). Recompiling is not realistic on managed services, so keep names short.

**Columns per table.** A table can have at most 1,600 columns, according to the limits page. The same row says this is further limited by the tuple having to fit on a single page, and I did not read the "see note below" text itself. The fetched summary of it says the heap page is 8192 bytes by default and that dropped columns still count toward the 1,600 (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). In practice, wide tables with large fixed-width types hit the page limit well before 1,600, and long-lived tables with many dropped columns lose headroom. Neither is likely to matter for a normally designed schema.

**Default max_connections.** The connection-settings documentation says "The default is typically 100 connections, but might be less if your kernel settings will not support it (as determined during initdb)" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html). So 100 is the usual default, but a given installation could have a lower value. Check it on the actual target with `SHOW max_connections;`. Managed providers often override the default, so confirm with yours. Some of the 100 slots are also reserved for superusers, so the application never gets all of them. I did not verify the size of that reservation here.

**Implications for the pool.** Each Postgres connection is a separate server process with its own memory cost. Total pool size across all service instances, plus migrations, monitoring and admin sessions, has to stay comfortably under max_connections. If you run many instances, size each instance's pool as a fraction of the total budget rather than using a large per-instance default.

**Recommendation.** Keep identifiers well under 63 bytes (aim for 50 or less to leave room for generated suffixes). Design tables far below the 1,600-column ceiling. Treat 100 connections as the planning budget unless you've confirmed otherwise, and size the combined pools to use well under that, adding an external pooler such as PgBouncer if you expect many instances.

{"answers": {"1": "63 bytes (NAMEDATALEN 64 minus 1)", "2": "1,600 columns (can be lower due to page-size limit)", "3": "100 (typically; may be lower depending on kernel settings at initdb)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html", "https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html"], "2": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html"]}}

**Research note: PostgreSQL memory and WAL defaults**

I read the official PostgreSQL documentation pages ("current" version) for all three settings.

**work_mem.** The default is 4MB. The documentation says "The default value is four megabytes (4MB)." (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). The limit applies per sort or hash operation, not per query or per connection. A single complex query, or many concurrent sessions, can therefore use many multiples of it. That is why the default is conservative.

**shared_buffers.** The default is typically 128MB. The documentation says "The default is typically 128 megabytes (128MB), but might be less if your kernel settings will not support it (as determined during initdb)." (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). So a fresh install on a constrained host may show a lower value. Check `SHOW shared_buffers;` rather than assuming 128MB.

**max_wal_size.** The default is 1GB. The documentation says "The default is 1 GB." It is a soft limit that can be exceeded under heavy load. (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html). A value without units is read as megabytes. In `pg_settings` you may see a raw number in a different internal unit, so read it with units via `SHOW max_wal_size;`.

**Caveats.** I read the "current" docs pages, so these values are the defaults for the latest release. Older major versions may differ, especially for `max_wal_size`, which was raised from 128MB to 1GB in 9.5. Managed services such as Azure and RDS often override these defaults. Confirm against your own server with `SHOW`.

**Recommendation.** Raise `shared_buffers` to about 25% of RAM on a dedicated database host. Raise `max_wal_size` (several GB is common for write-heavy workloads) so checkpoints are triggered by time rather than WAL volume. Keep `work_mem` modest globally and raise it per session or per role for the specific heavy queries that need it.

**Research note: DuckDB vs SQLite as a side-store next to PostgreSQL, and MERGE on PostgreSQL 15**

**DuckDB memory.** DuckDB's configuration reference lists the default `memory_limit` (alias `max_memory`) as 80% of system RAM (source: https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/configuration/overview.html). The older stable URL I tried first only redirected to that page. The default is generous, so if the analytics store shares a host with PostgreSQL, set an explicit lower limit. Otherwise the two will compete for memory.

**SQLite file size.** The SQLite limits page says a database file can hold at most 4294967294 pages. At the maximum page size of 65536 bytes, that is about 281 terabytes (256 tebibytes). At the default 4096-byte page size, the same page states about 17.5 terabytes (source: https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html). For almost any side-store, the file size limit will not matter in practice. Concurrency and analytical query speed are more likely to be the constraint.

**MERGE in PostgreSQL.** The PostgreSQL 15 release notes list "Support for the SQL MERGE command" as the first highlighted feature. The detailed entry describes it as similar to `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` but more batch-oriented (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/release-15.html). The PostgreSQL 15 manual also has a page for the command, which it describes as conditionally inserting, updating or deleting rows (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/sql-merge.html). So MERGE is available on 15 and was first included in version 15. The 15 manual page does not itself say which version introduced it. I got that from the release notes, and I assume 14 and earlier lack the command because the release notes list it as new in 15.

**Recommendation.** Choose DuckDB if the side-store will run aggregations and scans over large tables, because it is built for columnar analytics. Choose SQLite only if you need a small embedded file for light or mostly transactional use. Either way, MERGE is usable on PostgreSQL 15 for upserts and batch syncs, and on DuckDB, set the memory limit explicitly if it shares a host with PostgreSQL.

{"answers": {"1": "80% of system RAM", "2": "about 281 TB (at 65536-byte page size; ~17.5 TB at default 4096)", "3": "PostgreSQL 15"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/configuration/overview.html"], "2": ["https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/release-15.html", "https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/sql-merge.html"]}}

**Research note: TLS versions, DNS label length and HTTP 418**

**1. TLS 1.3.** The RFC that specifies TLS 1.3 has changed, so the answer depends on when you look. RFC 8446, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3", is the long-standing answer. Its abstract says it "specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446). The same page now marks RFC 8446 as obsolete and points to RFC 9846. RFC 9846 has the same title and is dated July 2026. It is a Proposed Standard, and its abstract says it "obsoletes RFC 8446, which specified TLS 1.3." It also obsoletes RFC 5246, which is TLS 1.2. Section 1.2 describes it as a minor update that keeps the same version number and stays backward compatible with RFC 8446 (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846). The current normative reference is therefore RFC 9846, and RFC 8446 is the historical one. Many existing documents and tools still cite RFC 8446.

**2. DNS label length.** A single label is limited to 63 octets. RFC 1035 section 3.1 says the length field leaves six usable bits, which "limit the label to 63 octets or less" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035). I only read the label limit from the page. I did not verify the overall name limit of 255 octets there. The 63-octet limit applies to each dot-separated component, not to the whole host name.

**3. "I'm a teapot".** This is HTTP status code 418. It is defined in section 2.3.2 of RFC 2324, "Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP/1.0)", an Informational RFC by L. Masinter dated 1 April 1998 (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324). It began as an April Fools' joke. I tried to confirm how the current HTTP specification, RFC 9110, treats 418, but the part of the page I could read did not reach the status code section. I make no claim about whether 418 is reserved or unused there.

**Recommendation.** Cite RFC 9846 as the current TLS 1.3 specification, mentioning RFC 8446 as its predecessor, and require every DNS label to be 63 octets or fewer. Do not use 418 in production services, since it comes from a joke RFC and has no real HTTP semantics.

{"answers": {"1": "RFC 9846 (current; obsoletes RFC 8446, the original TLS 1.3 RFC)", "2": "63 octets", "3": "418, defined in RFC 2324"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446", "https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846"], "2": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035"], "3": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324"]}}

**Research note: limits for the deploy runbook**

**Lambda timeout.** AWS's Lambda documentation says the default timeout is 3 seconds, adjustable in 1-second steps up to a maximum of 900 seconds (15 minutes). The console instructions repeat this, saying to set a value between 1 and 900 seconds (source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html). The same page adds a carve-out. Functions on Lambda Managed Instances can go up to 5,400 seconds (90 minutes), but only for asynchronous invocations and event source mapping invocations, with a couple of exceptions (same source). For a standard function, the ceiling is 900 seconds. Callers may impose shorter limits of their own, such as API Gateway in front of the function. I didn't read a page on that, so check it separately.

**Kubernetes grace period.** The Kubernetes Pod termination page says: "The default `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting is 30 seconds." It also says that "By default, all deletes are graceful within 30 seconds," and that `kubectl delete --grace-period=<seconds>` overrides this (source: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-termination/). The 30 seconds covers the `preStop` hook and the container's SIGTERM handling together. The fetch tool returned only the first 100,000 of about 106,000 characters of that page. The statements I quote were within that part.

**Docker docker0 subnet.** The default is 172.17.0.0/16, but I could not find a Docker page that states this outright. Docker's networking overview lists its built-in default address pools, and the first entry is `{ "base": "172.17.0.0/16", "size": 16 }` (source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/). That page does not itself say docker0 uses that pool. The bridge driver page shows a container on the default bridge with `inet 172.17.0.2/16` (source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/bridge/). That page also says the subnet can be changed with the `bip` setting in `daemon.json`, with `192.168.1.1/24` as its example. Together these support 172.17.0.0/16 as the default, but that is an inference. A search-result summary stated it plainly, but that summary came from secondary guides. I did not open those guides, so I don't cite them. The `dockerd` reference page gave no default value for `bip` (I fetched https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/dockerd/ but it does not state the subnet, so I don't list it as a source for this answer). If the runbook needs this stated with certainty, confirm it on a real host with `docker network inspect bridge`.

**Recommendation.** Set the runbook's shutdown budgets from the strictest platform: handlers should finish well inside 30 seconds on Kubernetes, with an explicit `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` if drain needs longer. Any Lambda work should stay under 900 seconds. Also note that 172.17.0.0/16 can collide with VPN or corporate ranges on developer machines, in which case set `bip` in `daemon.json`.

{"answers": {"1": "900 seconds (15 minutes)", "2": "30 seconds", "3": "172.17.0.0/16 (inferred from Docker's docs; not stated outright)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html"], "2": ["https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-termination/"], "3": ["https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/", "https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/bridge/"]}}

**Research note: test and tooling defaults**

**Vitest per-test timeout.** The default `testTimeout` is 5,000 ms in Node.js. It rises to 15,000 ms when `browser.enabled` is true (source: https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout). If our suites run in browser mode, the longer default applies. Anything slower than that needs an explicit override.

**Rust in the Linux kernel.** Linux 6.1 was the first mainline release with Rust support. The KernelNewbies page for that release says: "This release adds support for the Rust programming language." It describes this as initial support that later releases would improve (source: https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1). I first tried the kernel's own Rust documentation index, but it didn't say which version came first. The version claim therefore rests on KernelNewbies, a secondary source, rather than on kernel.org. Also, the Rust-support page I did read is for a 7.4.0-rc3 documentation build, so Rust in the kernel has moved on a lot since 6.1. The team should follow a much newer kernel than 6.1 if it needs current Rust features.

**PostgreSQL statement_timeout.** The default is zero, which disables the timeout. Unitless values are read as milliseconds. The documentation advises against setting it in `postgresql.conf`, because that would affect every session (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html). By default, nothing stops a runaway query.

**Recommendation.** Keep the vitest default of 5,000 ms and override it per test or per project only where a test needs longer. Set `statement_timeout` per role or per session for application connections instead of globally, and pin the kernel baseline to a recent release rather than 6.1.

{"answers": {"1": "5000 ms (15000 ms in browser mode)", "2": "Linux 6.1", "3": "0 (disabled)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout"], "2": ["https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html"]}}
